title: 'Mom might have calmed him down': Intervention might have averted death of mentally ill man, nurse tells inquiry
article: The inquiry into the death of a mentally ill man who died after he struggled with police concluded Monday following testimony from his case manager and his psychiatrist.

Kasim Cakmak, 37, died May 11, 2001, after being pepper- sprayed and handcuffed when police were called to the Alberta Mental Health Board's downtown outpatient centre to help transport Cakmak, who had schizophrenia, to Alberta Hospital Edmonton because he had been acting aggressively.

Darlene Pott, a registered psychiatric nurse, testified that she had been Cakmak's case manager for the five years before his death. Of all the staff at the centre, she said she knew him best. She was not working that day.
If staff had tried to contact her the day of his death, she would have approached the situation differently before it escalated. "I would have suggested that they try and contact the mom."

Pott had developed a working relationship with Cakmak that involved seeing him every one to two months, usually in the company of his mother, who would interpret. Cakmak had come from Turkey in 1991 and had difficulty with English. She said Cakmak's mother could calm him down when he became agitated.
Pott would also communicate with him using sign language and simple English words. Pott noted, however, it's standard practice for clinic staff not to contact family.

She did not believe it was written policy and thinks her co- workers responded appropriately. She said case managers can make a note in client files to flag problems such as allergies and extreme aggression, but she didn't feel there was a need to have a note to contact Cakmak's family if there was a problem with him.
Alberta's chief medical examiner earlier testified that Cakmak died from excited delirium, a rare condition in which extreme agitation creates an adrenalin rush that can stop the heart.
He said he doubted pepper spray contributed to his death.

Dr. Pierre Chue, the psychiatrist who treated Cakmak every couple of months from September 1999 to May 2001, said his schizophrenia fell into the range of the worst cases he has seen. Chue, who is clinical co-ordinator for community psychiatric programs for the mental health board, said Cakmak communicated in a nonsensical language.
"By virtue of his mental state, I don't think he knew what was going on around him."

In the months leading up to his death, he said Cakmak became more aggressive and even his mother was asking to have him committed to Alberta Hospital. Chue testified Cakmak was not benefiting from the day program and would have been better off in a group home, but his mother didn't want to put him in one.
He was on a number of drugs to control his condition, including an antipsychotic.

Chue said excited delirium is poorly understood and is rare. He's not sure what may have triggered it and Cakmak had not experienced it before. It's not possible to reason with an individual who is having an episode and more than half die from it. He said the only course of action is to keep the patient from hurting himself or others. Chue was not at the clinic the day Cakmak died.
A fatality inquiry cannot find guilt, but a judge can make recommendations to prevent such a death from occurring again.
